THE HUMAN ATLASES · DEEP DIVE

Silk Roads: changing networks of towns, ports and people

Silk Roads is a useful plural name for many overlapping connections. Cities, farms, ports and households made those connections possible. The playable scenes follow particular evidence through time, so an ancient port, a Sogdian letter and a Mongol-era handbook keep their own historical settings.

Selected evidence from 200 BCE to 1500 CE. This is a documented cross-section, not a claim to include every route or to date the beginning and end of Eurasian exchange.

Landscape and objects

The whole area in view

Eastern Mediterranean, Red Sea, Central Asia, South Asia and China. Archaeological phases and dated textual reports appear separately; connections are schematic examples of changing networks.

  1. Chang’an: foundation of Weiyang Palace

    200 BCE: reported palace construction

    Weiyang Palace places a major Han political center at the eastern end of later exchange corridors. A palace-construction date is not the birth date of an entire transcontinental network. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [8] [4] [5]

    Map reference: 34.3044°, 108.8572°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  2. Taxila: the foundation of Sirkap

    About 150 BCE; mid-second century BCE

    The fortified Sirkap settlement illustrates urban development at a South Asian crossroads. 150 BCE is a display anchor for 'mid-second century BCE', not an exact founding year. The wider Taxila landscape is much older. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [20]

    Map reference: 33.756°, 72.83°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  3. Luoyang: Eastern Han capital

    Eastern Han period, 25–220 CE

    Luoyang anchors an imperial urban phase at the eastern end of the corridor system. The interval selects one capital phase; it is not the complete lifespan of Luoyang. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [9] [5]

    Map reference: 34.7311°, 112.6214°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  4. Palmyra: caravan oasis and monumental city

    First–second centuries CE

    The surviving urban ensemble reflects connections between local, Mediterranean and Persian traditions. Architectural influence is not proof that every resident or object travelled the whole distance to China. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [21]

    Map reference: 34.551°, 38.267°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  5. Berenike: a Red Sea trading port

    Periplus context: mid-to-late first century CE

    The Periplus begins its maritime geography with Egyptian Red Sea ports including Berenike. This is a broad textual activity window, not the foundation date of the port. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [22] [11]

    Map reference: 23.91°, 35.47°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  6. Cana: Arabian incense and sea connections

    Periplus context: mid-to-late first century CE

    The Periplus describes Cana receiving incense from inland and trading with Indian and Persian ports. Bir Ali is an approximate locality identification; the narrative does not establish a timeless shipping lane. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [22]

    Map reference: 14.03°, 48.33°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  7. Barygaza: navigation and local expertise

    Periplus context: mid-to-late first century CE

    The account describes river pilots helping ships negotiate the approach to Barygaza, near modern Bharuch. The source describes particular commercial conditions; it is not a census or a complete port history. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [22]

    Map reference: 21.7°, 72.99°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  8. Niya: documents from an oasis society

    Approximately 235–325 CE

    Kharosthi documents preserve administration and everyday transactions in the Niya oasis region. Dates describe the document corpus; its people and institutions cannot be reduced to passing caravans. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [10] [11]

    Map reference: 37.95°, 82.7°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  9. Near Dunhuang: the Sogdian Ancient Letters

    Approximately 313–314 CE

    Letters recovered west of Dunhuang connect merchant households, distant business and interrupted communications. The findspot is represented near the western frontier corridor, not the town center. Dating is a scholarly reconstruction. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [12]

    Map reference: 40.35°, 93.87°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  10. Mogao: a long sequence of Buddhist caves

    From 366 CE; principal sequence through the fourteenth century

    Cave temples and manuscripts document many centuries of religious and artistic activity near Dunhuang. The endpoint rounds the end of the fourteenth century; individual caves have different dates and later histories. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [13]

    Map reference: 40.04°, 94.81°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  11. Ancient Penjikent: an inhabited Sogdian town

    Fifth–eighth centuries CE

    Excavation reveals houses, temples, workshops and monumental art in an urban settlement. The broad archaeological interval is not an exact foundation-to-destruction chronology. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [16] [6]

    Map reference: 39.487°, 67.624°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  12. Suyab: a changing urban and religious center

    Sixth–eleventh centuries CE

    Archaeology at Ak-Beshim documents a city with Buddhist, Christian and other religious material. The broad period includes rebuilding and political change; cultural labels do not identify a uniform population. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [14] [5]

    Map reference: 42.8019°, 75.2033°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  13. Balasagun: a Chuy valley city

    Tenth–fourteenth centuries CE

    Burana represents the medieval city of Balasagun and its surviving religious architecture. A broad occupation interval does not imply unchanged boundaries, rulers or population. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [15] [5]

    Map reference: 42.7467°, 75.2503°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  14. Bukhara: Samanid architectural evidence

    Tenth century CE

    The Samanid mausoleum anchors an early medieval architectural phase in Bukhara. The city predates this monument; much visible urban fabric belongs to later periods. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [18]

    Map reference: 39.777°, 64.41°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  15. Merv: Seljuk capital phase

    Eleventh–twelfth centuries CE

    Merv’s archaeological landscape includes a major Seljuk capital phase. This selected phase is only part of a much longer sequence of settlements in the oasis. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [19] [6]

    Map reference: 37.66°, 62.18°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  16. Quanzhou: a Song–Yuan maritime emporium

    Tenth–fourteenth centuries CE

    Ports, bridges, religious monuments and production sites document an extensive trading city and its hinterland. The component sites have different histories; the interval describes the emporium phase, not simultaneous construction. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [23] [24]

    Map reference: 24.906°, 118.59°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  17. Tana: a merchant handbook’s western starting point

    Handbook compiled around 1340 CE

    Pegolotti’s instructions start the overland journey to Cathay at Tana, near modern Azov. The approximate date belongs to the handbook; Pegolotti did not claim to have personally travelled this entire route. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [25]

    Map reference: 47.11°, 39.42°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  18. Urgench: a trading stop in Pegolotti

    Handbook compiled around 1340 CE

    The handbook recommends Urgench as a place where merchants could sell goods on the journey east. This is advice about a route, not a dated expedition or a measurement of traffic. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [25]

    Map reference: 42.32°, 59.16°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  19. Samarkand: Timurid urban development

    Fourteenth–fifteenth centuries CE

    The Timurid city’s monuments and plan represent a later phase of Central Asian urban connections. Samarkand’s older Afrasiab settlement has a separate history; this date range does not imply uninterrupted prosperity. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [17]

    Map reference: 39.655°, 66.975°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

A network changes with its users

The modern label gathers land and maritime exchanges under one name. It should not suggest that a single authority built one road, that silk was the only cargo, or that most merchants crossed the whole continent. UNESCO’s overview describes connections carrying goods and knowledge in multiple directions. The map makes that plurality visible through separate dated scenes. [3]

Two UNESCO corridor studies provide different geographical scales. Chang’an–Tianshan follows eastern capitals, oasis towns and mountain corridors. Zarafshan–Karakum follows a Central Asian chain toward Merv and distinguishes Sogdian, medieval Islamic and later phases. Neither study supplies a universal timetable for every settlement shown here. [4] [6]

The cities were more than stops

Weiyang Palace in Chang’an anchors an early Han political center, while Luoyang marks an Eastern Han capital phase. Farther southwest, Sirkap at Taxila was founded around the middle of the second century BCE. These are different kinds of urban evidence. Their dates should remain attached to the particular palace, city phase or foundation being described. [8] [9] [20]

Ancient Penjikent’s houses, temples and workshops show a town in which people lived and worked. Suyab adds another record of urban change, with excavated religious buildings and inscriptions. Balasagun’s later occupation and monuments belong to a distinct nearby settlement. A shared corridor did not make these places culturally identical or politically continuous. [16] [14] [15]

Small documents, human consequences

The Kharosthi documents from the Niya region preserve local administration and transactions. Their approximate 235–325 date range belongs to the corpus, not to the entire life of the oasis. Such records allow the map to include settled institutions alongside the better-known long-distance travellers. [10] [11]

The Sogdian Ancient Letters, dated about 313–314, reveal commercial connections and personal vulnerability together. Letters associated with Miwnay and her daughter expose abandonment and hardship; another reports disruption affecting distant business. A line from Samarkand’s commercial world toward the Dunhuang region represents those ties, not a known courier’s track. [12]

Ports required local knowledge and labour

The first-century Periplus connects Red Sea, Arabian and Indian markets. At Barygaza it describes difficult approaches and local pilots; at Cana it links maritime exchange with inland incense. These passages make navigation, water, timing and regional expertise part of the story. The sea connection is a selected commercial scene, not a permanent lane that every ship followed. [22]

Quanzhou’s tenth–fourteenth-century evidence moves the maritime view to China. The mapped heritage components include transport infrastructure, places of worship and manufacturing areas. A port’s overseas connections depended on work inland as well as ships offshore. The map dates the trading-city phase while acknowledging that its individual structures were built at different times. [23] [24]

Religion, art and the work of interpretation

At Mogao, cave temples and manuscripts preserve a long sequence beginning in the fourth century and extending through the fourteenth. They show that religious and intellectual activity belonged to the oasis landscape. Their varied dates matter: a millennium of artistic production should not appear as one event caused by a single caravan. [13]

Palmyra’s first–second-century monuments combine several architectural traditions at a caravan oasis. Bukhara’s Samanid mausoleum and Merv’s Seljuk phase represent later urban settings. Objects and buildings provide evidence of interaction, but a stylistic resemblance alone cannot reconstruct the ancestry, language or travel history of all the people who lived beside them. [21] [18] [19]

Read a merchant’s instructions as instructions

Around 1340, Pegolotti’s handbook described stages from Tana through Central Asia toward Cathay. It discussed practical needs such as interpreters and supplies. Its route belongs to a particular commercial and political setting; the author did not claim to have personally made the full journey. The two playable links isolate the western stages and the onward connection rather than inventing daily progress. [25]

The same distinction applies to Marco Polo. A report can contain useful knowledge of cities and markets without supplying a personal visit to every place it names. Compare the companion guide’s reported journey with these wider networks to see how one traveller’s narrative differs from a regional history. [2] [1]

The timeline stops; exchange does not

Samarkand’s fourteenth–fifteenth-century Timurid development closes this selection with another changing urban landscape. Older Afrasiab and the later city are related places with distinct material histories. Ending this study at 1500 is a choice of scope, not evidence that trade or cultural contact ended then. [17] [3]

All points are locality anchors. Broad centuries describe selected occupation or artistic phases; single years may instead locate the approximate date of a text. Population totals are omitted where no defensible settlement count was established. The linked maps identify heritage components and modern conservation extents, not historic ethnic territories or complete route surveys. [5] [7] [24]
